passage:
Tuesday

I'm writing this with my door locked.

In the lunch line today, Sanya from 9-C turned round and said, "Hey Tenzin, is it true your dad left because of your mum's shouting?"

My stomach just dropped. Like a lift. I told that to one person. One. Naveen, on the bench behind the gym, in August, when I cried for the first time about it.

I couldn't even answer Sanya. I walked out of the line without my food.

Naveen was at the other table, laughing with his cricket friends. He looked up. He looked away.

I keep thinking about all the times we walked home together. I thought I knew him better than anyone. Now it's like I'm remembering a stranger.

I feel stupid. And sad in a way that's hard to explain, like someone died but nobody did.

qa.q: Who asked Tenzin the question in the lunch line?
qa.a: Sanya from 9-C turned round and said it in the lunch line.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling when Sanya repeated the story?
qa.a: Tenzin felt a sudden drop of humiliation and shock, then a heavy grief at losing the friend Tenzin thought Naveen was.

qa.q: What could help Tenzin in the next day or two?
qa.a: Talking to a trusted adult, such as a parent or school counsellor, about both the story spreading and the hurt, rather than carrying it alone.

qa.q: How might Naveen have felt when he looked up and then away?
qa.a: Naveen likely felt ashamed and uncomfortable, knowing he had told the secret.

grounding: A diary shows a teen hearing a private story repeated by someone else, feeling humiliation and grief and seeing a trusted friend as a stranger.

"I'm going to post it, Didi. Keerthana told everyone about my crush. So I'll tell everyone what she did at Diwali."

Ishita was sitting on her bed with her phone, thumbs already moving.

Roshni didi took the phone gently out of her hand. "What did she do at Diwali?"

"Doesn't matter. Something she'd hate people knowing."

"And then what?"

"Then she'll know how it feels."

"And everyone will know two secrets instead of one. And tomorrow people will be talking about what you did, not what she did."

Ishita pulled her knees up. "So I just let her get away with it?"

"No. You wait one day. Tomorrow you decide: talk to her, or stop being friends. Either is fine. Just not tonight, when you're this angry."

Ishita stared at the ceiling. "I hate that you're right."

"I'll give your phone back at breakfast," said Roshni.

qa.q: What did Keerthana tell everyone?
qa.a: Keerthana told everyone about Ishita's crush.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling as she started typing the post?
qa.a: She felt furious and hurt, wanting Keerthana to feel the same humiliation.

qa.q: Why was waiting one day the wise move?
qa.a: Posting Keerthana's secret would have made Ishita the one in the wrong; waiting lets her choose calmly whether to talk or end the friendship.

qa.q: How might Roshni didi be feeling in this conversation?
qa.a: Roshni is probably protective and concerned, wanting to stop Ishita from doing something she'd regret.

grounding: A teen wants revenge by exposing her friend's secret, and an older sister helps her wait a day instead.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Class 9, Thursday.

Met Aadhya and Farida together, at Farida's request, after Aadhya shared Farida's private message with the class group.

Aadhya began by saying, "It was a joke. Farida's overreacting. Everyone shares screenshots." Farida's face shut down.

I asked Aadhya to look at Farida and describe what she did, just the facts. There was a long silence. Then Aadhya's voice changed. "I took a screenshot of something you told only me. I sent it to thirty people. It was wrong." She stopped, then added, "I'm ashamed. I don't know why I did it."

Farida said nothing for a moment. Then she said, "That's the first time you haven't made it my fault."

Neither was ready to be friends again today. Agreed next step: Aadhya will ask the class group to delete the screenshot, and we'll meet again in a week.

qa.q: How many people did Aadhya send the screenshot to?
qa.a: Aadhya sent it to thirty people.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling when her voice changed?
qa.a: She felt ashamed, finally facing what she had done instead of hiding behind 'it was a joke'.

qa.q: Why did the second answer work better than the first?
qa.a: Naming the act as wrong, without calling Farida oversensitive, took real responsibility and made Farida feel heard.

qa.q: How did Farida react to Aadhya's real apology?
qa.a: Farida seemed to feel acknowledged, saying it was the first time Aadhya hadn't blamed her, though she wasn't ready to be friends yet.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a teen move from 'you're overreacting' to naming what she did as wrong and admitting shame.

passage:
Chaitanya, you're upset about Rohan telling your secret? Your Madhuri Mausi has a story for you.

When I was fifteen, my friend Kamala told the whole class that I was scared of water. Everyone laughed at the swimming lesson.

A week later she came to me, crying. She said, "I did it to be popular. I'm sorry. I won't do it again." I didn't trust her all at once. For a long time I didn't tell her anything big. But she kept her word. Year after year. By college, we were close again, though not in the same easy way.

Then there was another girl, Leena. She did something similar, and when I told her, she laughed and said I was too sensitive. I stopped being her friend. Quietly, no drama. I found better friends.

Both endings were right, beta. It depends on what they do next.

qa.q: What did Kamala tell the whole class?
qa.a: Kamala told the class that Madhuri was scared of water.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling after Kamala's apology?
qa.a: She was touched by the apology but still wary, so she kept her big secrets to herself for a long time.

qa.q: What choices inside the story made the two endings different?
qa.a: Kamala apologised sincerely and kept her word, so a slower friendship returned; Leena laughed it off, so Madhuri ended the friendship calmly.

qa.q: How might Kamala have felt through those years of being trusted slowly?
qa.a: Kamala probably felt some regret and patience, knowing she had to earn Madhuri's trust back over time.

grounding: An elder recalls one friendship slowly rebuilt after a real apology and another ended with dignity when the friend shrugged it off.

It was 11 p.m. at the office, the air conditioning had died with the power, and the client deck was due at eight in the morning.

Elizabeth sat on the floor of the conference room with her laptop on a chair, and Shankar handed her a torch.

"Remember our first week here?" he said. "Four years ago. Neither of us knew how to use the printer."

She laughed, then went quiet. Shankar had driven her to the hospital the night her mother had surgery. He'd listened to her cry on the fire escape after her breakup, and never once said "I told you so."

"You're the only person here I can be a total mess around," she said.

"Likewise," said Shankar, sliding her a packet of biscuits. "Now. Slide nine is ugly."

By three, the deck was done. By then she was too tired to be anything but herself, and it didn't matter.

qa.q: Where did Shankar drive Elizabeth on the night of her mother's surgery?
qa.a: He drove her to the hospital.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling when she told Shankar he's the only person she can be a mess around?
qa.a: She felt safe and grateful, trusting him completely after years of support.

qa.q: What keeps friendships like this strong?
qa.a: Showing up in hard moments, listening without judging and working side by side, as Shankar did, builds deep trust.

qa.q: How might Shankar feel about their friendship?
qa.a: Shankar seems to value it just as much, saying 'likewise' and easing the pressure with biscuits and humour.

grounding: During a late-night deadline, two long-time colleagues show years of mutual support, where one can be at her weakest without judgement.

"So you'll recommend me?" Jeevan asked, leaning into the manager's cabin.

"The team lead post is between you and Uday," said Mr Kulkarni. "Uday's strong."

Jeevan felt the old fear rise: another year stuck while Uday moved up. Uday, who'd covered for him during his father's surgery. Uday, who'd told him, over beer last month, that he thought Kulkarni's targets were unrealistic.

"Sir," Jeevan heard himself say, "I just think the lead should believe in the targets. Uday's said privately he thinks they're... unrealistic."

Kulkarni's eyebrows went up. "Did he."

That evening, Jeevan's flatmate asked why he was so quiet.

"Just work."

"Did something happen?"

"Nothing. It's business. Everyone looks out for themselves." He turned the TV up. He didn't want to hear the word his mind kept offering him.

qa.q: What had Uday said privately about the targets?
qa.a: Uday had said he thought Kulkarni's targets were unrealistic.

qa.q: What was Jeevan afraid of when he spoke to Mr Kulkarni?
qa.a: He was afraid of being left behind, stuck another year while Uday moved up, and that fear overrode his loyalty.

qa.q: What turning point is still available to Jeevan?
qa.a: He could go back to Kulkarni and correct himself, and tell Uday honestly what he did, rather than calling it business.

qa.q: How might Uday feel if he learns what Jeevan said?
qa.a: Uday would likely feel shocked and betrayed, since he had supported Jeevan and shared the complaint in trust.

grounding: Afraid of being left behind for a promotion, a man reveals his friend's private complaint to the manager and calls it business, not betrayal.

I was in the pantry when Parul from HR said it, casually, stirring her tea. "Shame about your transfer request. Sameer mentioned to the director you'd been talking about leaving. That's probably why."

I said, "Oh," and carried my cup back to my desk.

For the rest of the afternoon I felt nothing. I answered emails. I laughed at a meme. It was like my body had gone to sleep.

The anger came at 11 at night, at home, so hard I sat up in bed. Sameer. Who I'd told about my transfer plan because he was my closest friend at work. Sameer, who'd come to my father's funeral.

And under the anger, something worse. I wasn't only losing a friend. I was losing the man I thought he was. That man never existed, maybe.

I'm Farida, and I'm twenty-six, and it felt like grief.

qa.q: Who told Farida about Sameer?
qa.a: Parul from HR told Farida, in the pantry.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling in the afternoon compared to 11 at night?
qa.a: In the afternoon Farida felt numb, as if asleep; at night a strong rage came, with grief underneath.

qa.q: What could Farida do before confronting Sameer?
qa.a: Farida could give the anger a night to settle, talk it over with someone trusted, and then ask Sameer for a direct, private conversation.

qa.q: How might Parul have seen the pantry moment?
qa.a: Parul seemed to think it was known or casual news, probably unaware it would shock Farida.

grounding: A young adult learns from a third person that a close colleague was disloyal, feels numb then furious, and grieves the friend they thought they had.

Nirmala booked the small meeting room on the fourth floor for fifteen minutes and sent Sabina an invite: "Can we talk, just us?"

Sabina came in with her notebook, smiling uncertainly.

Nirmala had written what she wanted to say on a sticky note, so her voice wouldn't wobble. "Last Monday, in the leadership review, you told Arvind I'd missed the vendor deadline. You knew I'd flagged the delay two weeks earlier. You were there when I flagged it."

Sabina started to speak. Nirmala raised a hand gently. "Let me finish. I felt humiliated, and I felt like I lost a friend that day. I'm not going to make a scene. But I need to know why."

The room was very quiet. Sabina put her notebook down.

"I was scared about my own review," she said finally. "It was wrong."

Nirmala nodded. She didn't smile. But she stayed.

qa.q: How long did Nirmala book the meeting room for?
qa.a: She booked it for fifteen minutes.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling going into the meeting?
qa.a: She was nervous enough to write notes so her voice wouldn't wobble, but determined to speak clearly about her hurt.

qa.q: Why was a private, direct conversation a wise choice?
qa.a: It let Nirmala describe the facts and her feelings without a public scene, giving Sabina room to answer honestly.

qa.q: How might Sabina have felt when Nirmala raised her hand and kept speaking?
qa.a: Sabina was likely uncomfortable and ashamed, which led her to admit fear and that it was wrong.

grounding: In a workplace meeting room, a woman asks for a private talk and clearly describes what happened and how it felt, inviting an honest answer.

Rekha had gone silent after Jeevan told their boss about her plan to resign, and now, two weeks later, she'd agreed to meet him at the tea stall outside the Andheri station.

Jeevan had rehearsed two speeches on the train. One began, "Look, I was under a lot of pressure." The other began, "I was wrong."

When Rekha sat down, looking tired and guarded, the first speech came into his mouth. He felt hot, exposed, like everyone at the stall could see.

He swallowed it.

"I told Kapoor because I wanted him to see me as loyal. It cost you your bonus. I'm ashamed of it." He pushed an envelope across. "I've written to Kapoor saying I misrepresented what you said. This is a copy."

Rekha read it slowly. She didn't forgive him. But she didn't leave, either.

qa.q: Where did Rekha agree to meet Jeevan?
qa.a: At the tea stall outside the Andheri station.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling when the first speech came into his mouth?
qa.a: He felt hot and exposed, torn between defending himself and owning his shame.

qa.q: Why does the letter to Kapoor matter more than just saying sorry?
qa.a: It is a real amend that corrects the damage, showing Jeevan is willing to face consequences, not just protect his image.

qa.q: How might Rekha be feeling as she reads the letter?
qa.a: Rekha is guarded and still hurt, but the letter may give her a first reason to consider whether trust can return.

grounding: A man who betrayed a colleague feels exposed and torn, then chooses remorse and a real amend over defending his image.

passage:
January: Mehak met Pallavi for coffee for the first time since Pallavi had shared her engagement news before Mehak was ready. Pallavi apologised again. Mehak said, "I believe you. We're okay." She meant it. But on the walk home, she noticed she hadn't told Pallavi about her new job.

March: At a friend's birthday dinner, Pallavi asked about Mehak's wedding plans. Mehak smiled and said, "Still early," and changed the subject. It wasn't coldness. She simply had decided which things she shared, and with whom.

June: They met for Pallavi's birthday. It was warm and cordial. They laughed about college. Mehak went home without resentment, and without the old ache either. The friendship had a new, shallower shape. She found she was at peace with it, and grateful for what it had once been.

qa.q: What did Mehak not tell Pallavi about in January?
qa.a: Mehak didn't tell Pallavi about her new job.

qa.q: How did Mehak feel after Pallavi's birthday in June?
qa.a: She felt at peace and grateful, without resentment, accepting the friendship's new shape.

qa.q: What did Mehak do well in rebuilding this friendship?
qa.a: She forgave sincerely but set clear limits on what she shared, which let the friendship continue safely.

qa.q: How might Pallavi experience the friendship now?
qa.a: Pallavi may notice Mehak shares less and feel a slight distance, but also relief that they are still friends.

grounding: Over months a friendship returns as cordial and careful, with limits on what is shared, and she lets go of bitterness.
